Yahtzee is still out there being mean about videogames, and good for him
items.summary: Zero Punctuation was an essential watch back in the day. Its successor Fully Ramblomatic still carries the torch.
items.body: When the HMS Escapist sank everyone worth a damn swam away to form a YouTube channel called Second Wind , where Yahtzee Croshaw's video series Zero Punctuation continued under the name Fully Ramblomatic. It's not exactly the same—the people have glasses now—but it's continuing the essential work of being rude about videogames on the internet. Back in the Before Times, when someone brought a videogame magazine to school we'd all gather round to flick through it, and the only measure of whether it was a good videogame magazine was if the captions on the screenshots were funny. I didn't notice until years later, but that meant we only read the British ones. That particularly British tone is something Yahtzee's videos share. It might come across as flippant to some, but to me it's always read as deep care. Putting in the effort to make a description witty instead of plain means you're working harder to keep your audience engaged, and doing that for videogames suggests you care enough about them to want your audience to actually pay attention. Yahtzee does that. Like Blackadder finding the 100th way to tell Baldrick he's an idiot, he never runs out of ways to complain about videogames.…

items.summary: الفريق الأبيض أهدر عدة فرص بعد الهدف الأول

items.title: Nier creator Yoko Taro says he's achieved his career dreams, but he continues working because it's 'good for preventing dementia'
items.summary: "With Drakengard, the first game I was given the opportunity to direct, I was actually able to do almost everything the way I wanted."
items.body: They say that art is never finished, only abandoned—but that doesn't seem to be the case for Yoko Taro, creator of Nier and Drakengard, who you might recognize by the round, smiley Emil mask he wears. According to a report from Denfaminicogamer (via IGN ), Taro said at the Tokyo French Institute last month that he's already more or less realized his vision and has considered retiring. "With Drakengard, the first game I was given the opportunity to direct, I was actually able to do almost everything the way I wanted," Taro said. "As a game otaku, I think the dream is to release something you've always wanted to create into the world. Having achieved that dream, I view everything after that as the remainder of my life." As for why he continues to work in gamedev if he's already achieved his dreams, well, he said the money doesn't hurt—and that he has a fear of how his mental health might degrade should he grow idle. "This is good for preventing dementia," he said. It's worth noting that Taro is, to put it in technical terms, a bit of a silly goose, if the mask didn't tip you off. If I festooned myself with garish lights, how would I scavenge for supplies in a frozen wasteland without being spotted by strangers who may or may not kill me before I can use my grappling hook to get away? This isn't a real problem I have, nor is it a real problem Arc Raiders players will have anymore, since your backpack now has an emissive toggle. items.title: RPGs are simply better when you're an idiot
items.summary: I just can't relate to these capable heroes.
items.body: Dungeon Master (Image credit: Future) Welcome to Dungeon Master , PC Gamer's regular RPG column, where Online Editor Fraser Brown delves into PC gaming's most beloved and enduring genre. Grab a seat in our badly-lit tavern and please ignore the goblin puke. Most videogame RPGs are selling a power fantasy—the idea that you are competent, clever and regardless of the odds will still manage to save the day. Fate has made you a hero, and nothing is going to stop you from achieving your goals. And this holds a lot of appeal. It's sometimes nice to be able to take a holiday from my own incompetence. Over the last few days I've managed to drop my dinner, get trapped on a bus going in the wrong direction, get peed on by a dog, get almost run over by a car and, to top it all off, actually get knocked over by an electric scooter. I am a walking disaster. (Image credit: BioWare) Geralt never gets peed on. Shepard never lands on their arse after colliding with a teen. These are not heroic moments. items.title: This Control-inspired action game set in a 'planet-scale alien mind' has one of the most stunning art styles I've seen this year
items.summary: Studio Lifeforms' Etre is shaping up to be a visual feast.
items.body: In the age of near photorealism, it takes a lot for a game's visuals to impress me. As cramming yet more pixels into a videogame character's face provides diminishing returns, standing out from the crowd is increasingly about how creative developers get in applying that power. All that said, I was genuinely mesmerised by the debut footage of Etre , an upcoming action adventure game with a truly eye-popping art style. Created by LA-based developer Studio Lifeforms, Etre is a narrative driven-action game set on Orbis, which Studio Lifeforms describes as a "planet-scale alien mind on the brink of awakening". You play as a character named Xyle, who arrives at this sentient cityscape in search of his soulmate Atel. According to Studio Lifeforms, the game's distinctive visuals are inspired by graphic novels of the '70s and '80s. Studio Lifeforms doesn't specify which graphics novels, and I am too much of a comics philistine to tell you. But the result is an incredibly distinctive visual style. items.body: Disk Cleanup (Image credit: Future) Welcome to Disk Cleanup , our regular weekend feature delving into the PCs of PC gaming luminaries. Come back every weekend to read a new interview, digging into the important questions, like "How tidy is your desktop?" and "What game will you never uninstall?" SungWon Cho got into PC gaming through the children's adventure games developed by Humongous Entertainment. "Games like Freddi Fish, Spy Fox, those really stuck with me," says the YouTuber and actor. items.body: Weird Weekend Weird Weekend is our regular Saturday column where we celebrate PC gaming oddities: peculiar games, strange bits of trivia, forgotten history. Pop back every weekend to find out what Jeremy, Josh and Rick have become obsessed with this time, whether it's the canon height of Thief's Garrett or that time someone in the Vatican pirated Football Manager . For most of PC gaming history, there were three states of PC game—your regular old video game, expansions/DLC, and mods. But for a brief period in the 1990s, there was a fourth state, the level pack—collections of levels for the early first-person shooters like Duke Nukem 3D and Quake . These level packs were sold on shelves as boxed products just like their video game counterparts. But they occupied a far more amorphous position between the other three states of PC gaming. In form and structure, they were similar to expansions, and are sometimes bundled into the same category. The Master Levels for Doom 2, for example, are regarded as an official expansion to that game. I've been a long-term fan of Molyneux's games, though, stretching all the way back to Theme Park, so I also took this opportunity to also ask the legendary game dev about, arguably, his most famous god game creation to date, Black & White . And, specifically, I wanted to know where the origin of Black & White's most famous creations came from: the titanic animal creatures that you, as god, nurture in the game and use as an instrument of your will. items.summary: Not emulation or a remake, a native PC port of Kojima's horror classic has arrived.
items.body: One of the most beloved horror games (demos?) of all time is finally free from the shackles of the PS4. Hideo Kojima's P.T. has been natively ported to PC by programmer Lorean Xavier, who made the project public this week. Not an emulator nor a remake, the native PC client does not contain any copyrighted materials—it requires a dumped copy of P.T. to function—but instead translates the original code into something that'll run on Windows and Linux. That distinction not only sidesteps potential corporate scrutiny, but also allows Xavier to add modern graphical features and mod support to the PC version. It's an impressive effort that, according to the creator, has been in the works since 2024. "I wanted to make the version of P.T. that my younger self always wished existed," Xavier, 21, told PC Gamer over email. "My attachment to the game goes all the way back to my childhood. I remember watching videos of it on my phone, wishing I could experience it myself. I didn't have a PS4, so playing the original was never really an option for me. items.body: I just made a noise like air being slowly released from a balloon . It's been 17 years since the original Machinarium , a wordless tale of love in a crumbling city of robots. Amanita Design has put out some great games over that span— Botanicula , Chuchel , Creaks , Phonopolis —but hasn't breathed even a hint that more Machinarium might be on the way. So why now? "We're not getting any younger, and the world seems to be ending, so if we were ever going to make Machinarium 2, now is the right time," Amanita CEO and designer Jakub Dvorský said—a bit dark, sure, but I can't find any factual fault in his reasoning. "We're also grateful to every player who waited patiently all these years. We couldn't have done it without them."
